title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Price increase to $3.97 (+3.7%)
drivers.evidence: Two recent weeks at same price sold 27% and 40% below baseline; noise-adjusted price effect from past promotions suggests ~28% drop at this price point.

drivers.name: Store closure on Monday
drivers.evidence: One day closed in a 7-day week reduces potential sales by ~14%; no prior closure data, but typical for this store.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 124.1. The target week has no event, but a price increase to $3.97 (+3.7%) and a store closure on Monday. Price increases reduce demand; past promotions show price sensitivity, with no prior occurrence at this price. The 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-05 weeks (same price) sold 106 and 75 units—27% and 40% below baseline. The noise-adjusted effect of price increases is estimated at x0.72. The store closure on Monday (1/7 of the week) reduces potential sales by ~14%. Combining these: 0.72 × 0.86 = 0.62. The evidence is thin (few price spikes), so shrink toward 1.0. Final median multiplier: 0.75. Downside spread widened slightly due to uncertainty. Confidence: medium.

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.1 | 5%-95%: 77.2 - 200.6 | 10%-90%: 88.7 - 170.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
